This legal document is a civil complaint filed by the Government of the United States Virgin Islands (USVI) against JP Morgan Chase Bank in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, under the Trafficking Victims Protection Act, the Virgin Islands Criminally Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, and the Virgin Islands consumer fraud and deceptive business practices law. The plaintiff alleges that the financial institution knowingly and negligently facilitated, sustained, and concealed the human trafficking network operated by Jeffrey Epstein for more than a decade, turning his bank accounts into the financial axis used to pay recruiters and victims. The complaint argues that the bank ignored multiple financial alerts, suspicious transactions, and large cash withdrawals linked to the sexual exploitation of women and minors, prioritizing commercial benefits and the high-net-worth clients that Epstein allegedly brought to its private banking division, in coordination with senior executives.

This legal document is a civil complaint filed by Virginia L. Giuffre against Prince Andrew, formerly Duke of York, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, under New York’s Child Victims Act. The plaintiff alleges that she was a victim of sex trafficking and systematic abuse by Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell when she was a minor, and that, under coercion and implicit or express threats, she was forced to have sexual relations with the defendant on multiple occasions and in several places, including London, New York, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. The complaint argues that Prince Andrew acted deliberately, knowing that the plaintiff was a minor and a victim of trafficking, and adds that, after Epstein’s arrest and subsequent death, the defendant has avoided cooperating with U.S. authorities. On the basis of these facts, which the complaint characterizes as serious sexual offenses under New York criminal law, the plaintiff brings claims for battery and intentional infliction of emotional distress and seeks damages for the profound and lasting psychological harm suffered. The defendant denied the allegations, and the case ended in an out-of-court settlement in 2022 with no findings of fact.

title: Text Mining and Linguistic Network Analysis of Court Filings in the Epstein Case
text:
Methods
Each filing is analyzed with the same pipeline, implemented in R; the methods and their references are described in detail in the article:

Word frequency. The text is tokenized, punctuation and numbers are removed, the text is converted to lowercase, and stop words are filtered out. The most frequent terms are shown in a lollipop chart, with their absolute and relative frequencies, and in a word cloud.
Sentiment and emotions. Words are scored with the AFINN lexicon, from \(-5\) to \(5\), multiplied by their frequency; the terms with the largest contributions are shown in a bar chart and in a comparison word cloud of negative and positive words. Emotions are identified with the NRC lexicon (anger, anticipation, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, surprise, and trust) and shown in a pie chart.
Bigram network. Pairs of consecutive words (excluding pairs that contain a stop word) are counted, and those whose frequency is at least a document-specific threshold form an undirected weighted graph. The largest connected component is plotted with and without edge weights.
Skipgram network. Pairs of words that are consecutive or separated by one intermediate word are counted and form an undirected weighted graph. For its largest connected component, the following are reported: the most frequent skipgrams, global network statistics (mean distance, mean and standard deviation of the degree, clique number, density, transitivity, and degree assortativity), the ten words with the highest eigenvector centrality, and the communities found with the fast greedy algorithm.

Lexicons are general-purpose and may misclassify terms in legal language (for instance, United in United States is scored as positive), and they ignore negations. Results should be read with these limitations in mind.

In addition, terms such as “abuse” and “sex” point directly to the offenses alleged in the complaint. Sentiment analysis
Figure 3 shows that two words have a very high score: “abuse” and “victims”, since they combine a high frequency with a strongly negative value. These words dominate the negative sentiment and also the overall sentiment of the text, as the magnitude of their scores is far larger than that of the positive words. Other words with a moderate negative charge include “damages”, “destroy”, “abused”, “victim”, and “disgrace”, among others, showing that the negative sentiment is characterized by words denoting some form of harm.








Figure 3: Bar chart of sentiment scores: Giuffre v. Maxwell.





The prevailing positive words in the text are “powerful”, “helping”, “united”, “committed”, and “agreement”. However, their emotional charge is much lower than that of the negative words. Moreover, in this particular context, these terms are not necessarily used with a positive connotation. For example, “powerful” may refer to the economic and social power attributed to Maxwell and Epstein and how, according to the complaint, they used it to discredit Giuffre; likewise, “helping” may allude to the way in which, according to the complaint, Epstein and Maxwell facilitated the abuse, and “united” most likely comes from “United States”, the name of the court. It is therefore clear that the positive sentiment does not genuinely prevail in the text.








Figure 4: Pie chart of emotions: Giuffre v. Maxwell.





Figure 4 shows the percentage of words associated with each emotion in the text. The predominant emotion is anger, with 19%, which directly reflects the context of the case, a complaint for defamation and abuse. The same conflictive nature of the facts explains why other emotions such as disgust, fear, and sadness remain important, each above 12%, and why surprise and joy show the lowest levels. The high percentage of trust (18%), in turn, is due to the nature of the document, which constantly uses terminology referring to legal entities, institutional procedures, and the expectation of legal action to redress the harm.
In conclusion, the overall sentiment of the text is negative, dominated by words related to the alleged offenses, the harm caused to the victim, and defamation. The high scores and frequencies of these terms not only reflect the seriousness of the issues addressed, but also reveal the nature of the allegations in the text. The positive sentiment, by contrast, is very weak, almost nonexistent compared with the negative one, and the words that express it do not necessarily have a positive connotation in this context; on the contrary, some of them carry a negative one.

On these grounds, arguing that the statements constitute defamation and libel per se, the plaintiff demands a jury trial and seeks compensatory, consequential, and punitive damages for the psychological harm and the serious damage to her personal and professional reputation. The defendant denies the allegations.

Sentiment analysis
Figure 3 shows that the word “victims” stands out disproportionately, with a remarkably high score in the negative sentiment category. This indicates that, in the context of the document, it is a term with a high weight, both because of its frequency and because of its negative semantic charge. It also indicates that the text focuses not only on the plaintiff, but also on the alleged victims of this type of violence as a group. Another relevant feature of the negative profile of the text refers to the consequences of suffering these offenses, reflected in terms such as “damages”, “destroy”, “perjury”, and “intimidate”. Finally, there are words directly linked to the alleged acts and to the conduct of those involved, such as “abuse”, “abused”, “lied”, “refuse”, and “refused”, which describe the nature of the facts alleged.

Positive sentiment, on the other hand, is represented by a limited number of terms with very low scores; the only words that stand out are “powerful” and “committed”. This shows that positive sentiment is very weak or even nonexistent, since in the specific context of the document both terms do not necessarily denote positive aspects. On the one hand, the word “powerful” refers to the status and influence attributed to Epstein and Dershowitz, who, according to the complaint, had vast political, economic, and social power that allowed them to act without facing immediate legal consequences. On the other hand, the term “committed” may refer to Giuffre’s commitment to supporting people who have been victims of similar exploitation networks, or to the offenses committed.

Figure 4 shows that the predominant emotions are trust and anticipation, with 20% and 14%, respectively. This can be explained by the fact that one of the aims of the complaint is to redress the effects of the alleged offenses; under this premise, the structure of the text suggests that, beyond dwelling on the abuse, it seeks compensation for the harm. Nevertheless, emotions such as anger and fear, with 16% each, remain prominent in the document. This is due to the nature of an account told from the position of a victim, a context in which these reactions may arise. To a lesser extent, sadness and disgust also appear, which are expected emotions when describing sexual assault. Finally, the least frequent emotions are joy and surprise, which is entirely reasonable given that the text does not evoke them.
The tone of the text is almost entirely negative; positive sentiment is limited to two words that, in the specific context of the document, do not necessarily have a positive connotation. The overall tone is thus negative, complemented by the presence of emotions such as anger, fear, sadness, and disgust. However, despite this generally negative tone, emotions such as trust and anticipation stand out, suggesting an orientation towards seeking justice and full redress of the harm suffered by the victims.

Finally, there are no terms related to the redress sought for the plaintiff, even though this aspect had previously been identified as one of the relevant themes of the case.
The skipgram network is built with all pairs, regardless of their frequency, which makes it possible to find semantic relationships that are not perceptible at first sight. The largest connected component is also used, since it contains the most important information and allows the computation of statistics that are not defined on a disconnected graph, such as the mean distance between vertices.

Table 2 shows that the mean distance of the network is 5.14; that is, on average, slightly more than five steps are needed to go from one word to another. Being a moderate value, it suggests a less centralized narrative, in which the different concepts and actors are connected more gradually throughout the text. This interconnection is supported by the mean degree of 3.79, meaning that each word is directly connected to almost four different terms on average. However, the standard deviation of the degree is very high (7.79) compared with its mean, which reveals great variability: a few words are connected to many others, while most have very few connections. In other words, there are hub words that appear next to many different terms, which points to very marked themes in the text.
Regarding the grouping of words, the clique number is 6, meaning that the largest group of words that are all connected to each other has 6 terms; such a structure usually reflects a frequently repeated central argument or words that always appear together. At the global level, however, the density of the network is close to 0 (it rounds to 0.00), meaning that well under 1% of all possible connections are present; the network is therefore very sparse, as is usual in word networks with a large and varied vocabulary. Consistently with this sparsity, the transitivity is 0.06, so there is only a 6% probability that two words connected to the same term are also connected to each other (forming triangles), which reflects a structure with low cohesion. Finally, the degree assortativity is negative (-0.11), indicating a mild tendency of highly connected words to link with words that have few connections, rather than with other central words.
Table 3 shows that the most important words according to eigenvector centrality are “Ms” and “Pierson”, both with values close to 1 (the maximum value). This stands out when compared with the other words, none of which reaches 0.2, and confirms that Pierson is the central axis of the whole text and that all the themes are organized around her. People such as Black, Epstein, and Maxwell also appear, to a lesser extent, indicating that these actors are important in the general narrative. Finally, terms such as “called”, “refused”, and “told” appear, which refer directly to the alleged modus operandi of the trafficking network and to how Epstein and Black were related, making the relationship between these two men a relevant theme in the case.
